editorial_policy.verified_public_information: Descriptions are newly written original summaries of linked official public pages; not copied full source content.
editorial_policy.oral_tradition: Explicitly label named origin stories as oral accounts, legends or reported etymology.
editorial_policy.indigenous_communities: Do not convert geographic associations or a festival organizer’s account into a community-approved statement of ritual, belief, ethnicity or permission. Get FPIC and community review.
editorial_policy.dates: Annual festival listing is not a confirmed schedule for a particular year.
editorial_policy.statistics: Avoid stale town population, prices, opening hours and year-sensitive tourism counts.
editorial_policy.images: No images, recordings or protected writing texts are included; rights and consent must be separately checked.
editorial_policy.coverage: This is a substantial sourced draft, not an exhaustive ethnographic history of all localities.

localities.name: Baco
localities.lead: An early administrative and mission center close to Mount Halcon; banana agriculture and layered origin stories.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: The provincial municipal-history account describes Baco as one of the earliest Spanish-era administrative and church centers on Mindoro, before northern ecclesiastical activities shifted toward Calapan. It offers more than one account of Baco’s name: one connects it with the edible fern pako, and another with water-damaged or uneven roads. These should be presented as reported explanations, not proven etymology. Baco’s history includes shifts of the town center and settlement patterns connected to coastal conditions and flooding. Its administrative timeline in the online narrative contains complex dates, so any precise claim that Baco was the first capital should be checked against legal or archival records before becoming a scored quiz fact.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: Baco sits near Mount Halcon and contains mountain, river, farming and coastal landscapes. The municipal history describes recurring heavy rainfall and flooding, while the contemporary tourism directory lists Mount Halcon and river-related destinations. Banana production is prominent in the town’s official festival description. These physical and agricultural themes offer an opportunity to teach how rainfall, farms and access roads affect the experiences of communities, without implying that every resident has the same livelihood or that mountain trails are open for entry.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: The cultural directory includes Mangyan Cubool: Cultural Booth of Love, and local history discusses Iraya and Alangan connections in Baco. Those are clues for respectful research, not grounds for assigning one language or set of beliefs to every person. The Banana Festival provides a separate, public celebration of farm products that includes named social activities. Lessons can contrast a documented festival schedule with evidence about historic religious sites and cultural institutions. Avoid reproducing unverified beliefs or stories about particular Mangyan groups as if they were general community facts.

localities.name: Bansud
localities.lead: A younger municipality whose local narrative links river-delta settlement, farming and independence from Bongabong.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Bansud was formerly part of Bongabong. The tourism portal traces its separate municipal status to Republic Act No. 2514, approved in 1959; it reports July 4 as the date associated with municipal establishment and local foundation observances. The local-history page also records a story connecting the town name to basud, described as a river delta, and identifies migration by families from other Philippine islands. The name explanation belongs in an oral-history field until linguistically verified. Bansud’s administrative story differs from neighboring older towns because it centers on twentieth-century municipal separation.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The history page locates Bansud between mountains and the Tablas Strait and describes agricultural and fishing activities around its river and coastal settlement. The tourism directory also lists Bato Viewing Hills and waterways or waterfalls as attractions. The Basudani Festival is specifically related to giving thanks for local harvest abundance, which gives learners an entry into farming and collective civic celebration. Neither a river-delta story nor a crop-centered festival proves that all current Bansud residents work in agriculture.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Bansud Museum is listed among the province’s historical and cultural sites. This is a distinctive research anchor: the app can ask learners to compare public museum evidence, reported oral traditions about the name, and legal documentation of municipal formation. A museum listing by itself does not identify its entire collection, the provenance of objects, or permission to reuse photos. Put locally verified museum exhibits in an editable review queue rather than inventing collections or treating every old object as Indigenous.

localities.name: Bongabong
localities.lead: A farming and coastal municipality shaped by a river, historical town-name changes and access to national roads.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Bongabong’s municipal-history page recounts old names such as Binago, Sukol and Sumilang and connects the development of the settlement with the Bongabong River and a former town site at Anilao. The page explicitly acknowledges uncertainty in the origin of the name. It also describes repeated municipal reorganizations during the American period and growing settlement after improved highway access in the twentieth century. The page mentions both 1920 and 1927 in connection with local organization; this discrepancy should be resolved with primary government records before publication as a single exact founding date.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The municipal history associates Bongabong’s growth with cultivated agricultural land, coconut plantations along coastal plains, rattan and forest products, fishing, and the opening of road connections. Current tourist listings also include river features and farm-related destinations. The official SULYOG Festival focuses on banana and coconut crops, illustrating one way farmers’ products become part of a public celebration. These points should be taught as historical and festival-specific sources, not a present-day economic survey of every household.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Bongabong’s history is especially suitable for teaching source criticism: an oral river-name explanation is not the same kind of evidence as a law or map, and twentieth-century road building differs from the present-day festival calendar. The SULYOG name is interpreted by organizers using a Mangyan-associated word and Tagalog niyog. Learners should not generalize that word to all Mangyan languages without a community-reviewed linguistic source. Avoid generic accounts of Indigenous practices where no town-specific community source has been verified.

localities.name: Bulalacao
localities.lead: Southern island and maritime heritage with old-settlement archaeology, complex trade-history claims and coastal celebrations.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Bulalacao’s municipal history discusses earlier place names, coastal settlement and debates about the ancient place called Ma-i or Mait in historical accounts. Some proposed identifications are speculative: do not present Bulalacao as conclusively proven to be that trading site. The page reports archaeological work at Sitio Lobok, including remains interpreted as a historic fortified church settlement, and recounts changes in the municipal seat and separation of Mansalay. This gives Bulalacao a distinctive historical focus on settlement archaeology, shifting political boundaries and the difference between a hypothesis and a demonstrated fact.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The provincial tourism portal lists Aslom Island, Buyayao Island, Pocanil Rock Formation and Suguicay Island among Bulalacao’s coastal destinations. Such places invite learning about maritime routes, fishing and the care of island environments; they do not guarantee open public access, current boat schedules or the absence of environmental restrictions. The Biniray Festival connects the public observance of Saints Peter and Paul with sea-related thanksgiving, fluvial activities and traditions reported by festival organizers.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: The Library of Congress provides a different history link: collector Fletcher Gardner was stationed at Bulalacao in 1904–1905 and later collaborated with Mindoro residents Ildefonso and Eusebio Maliwanag on the history of written Mangyan materials. This fact connects the locality to the provenance of archival objects, not exclusive ownership of the manuscripts or the authors’ identities. Teaching Bulalacao can therefore link maritime trade hypotheses, archaeological method, living coastal experiences and documented manuscript history with separate citations for each.

localities.name: Calapan City
localities.lead: The provincial capital and a center for civic history, museums, Mangyan documentation and several distinct light celebrations.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: The municipal-history page traces changes in Calapan’s role under Spanish ecclesiastical and provincial administration and identifies the transfer of the provincial capital from Puerto Galera to Calapan in the nineteenth century. The PPDO identifies Calapan as the present capital of Oriental Mindoro. Republic Act No. 505 and subsequent implementation establish the modern provincial split in 1950, a government event rather than the beginning of Mindoro’s older cultures. The city’s contemporary role as a port, services center and seat of government is distinct from any single festival.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: Calapan connects the north Mindoro travel corridor with administration, education, commerce and cultural institutions. The tourism portal lists a number of museums and civic landmarks, but the pages titled Oriental Mindoro Heritage Museum include two different descriptions: one at the old Provincial Capitol in Ibaba East, and another for a museum at Calapan City Hall in Guinobatan. They should not be merged or given a single precise address without checking institutional names and contacts. The old Provincial Capitol museum page explains MAHAL TANA through Mangyan, Halcon, tamaraw and Naujan Lake.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Calapan hosts different festival records: Kalap relates to city identity and debated name explanations; Pandang Gitab is a province-level Festival of Lights; Fiesta MAHAL TANA brings municipal and city contingents together; Salong Dagitab emphasizes nighttime Christmas lighting. These are not four names for the same event. The Mangyan Heritage Center in Calapan is also an important place for public research and cultural advocacy, but its permission guidance explicitly states that the Center cannot grant blanket consent for community research or visits.

localities.name: Gloria
localities.lead: A town formed from parts of Pinamalayan, with bamboo, pottery and agricultural material culture.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Gloria’s municipal-history account traces settlement around Tambong and Maligaya, including migration from Marinduque and agricultural development along transport routes in the early twentieth century. Residents of a collection of barrios sought separate municipal status from Pinamalayan. The page describes multiple executive actions during the 1960s, a court decision that invalidated an earlier arrangement, and subsequent legislation recognizing the municipality. This sequence should be explained in chronological terms rather than reduced to one unverified single founding date.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The provincial account of Kawayanan Festival associates Gloria with bamboo cultivation alongside rice and coconut production. Its public destination listings include Bamboo Plantation, M. Adriatico Pottery and Agsalin Fish Sanctuary. Those entries point to several kinds of material and environmental heritage: bamboo products, pottery, coastal conservation and agricultural work. The list is a useful local directory, not a census of all craftsmen or a guarantee that visitors may collect objects or enter a sanctuary without permission.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Gloria is well suited to a lesson comparing a plant, a craft and an archive. Bamboo used in everyday objects is not automatically the same as a bamboo manuscript from the historical Mangyan writing collections. M. Adriatico Pottery is documented by name but the official listing does not independently establish the ancestry, dates or meaning of its ceramic designs. Learners should ask about makers, materials, specific practices and attribution, then explore how farms, coastal resources and public craft venues connect to the municipality’s identity.

localities.name: Mansalay
localities.lead: An important location for Hanunuo Mangyan writing and ambahan, with a dedicated heritage center and living communities.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: The provincial local-history account records nineteenth- and twentieth-century administration, mobility between coastal settlements and the eventual separate municipality of Mansalay under the interwar period. It also contains speculative early genealogies and origin legends that should be treated as oral narratives, not verified accounts of all Mangyan peoples. The town’s history should instead connect public administrative records with the voices of present communities. Panaytayan in Mansalay is especially important to the documented Hanunuo Mangyan poetic and writing tradition.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The Oriental Mindoro Heritage and Cultural Center is listed in Barangay B. del Mundo, Mansalay as an institution promoting understanding and preservation of Mangyan culture. The tourism portal also lists coastal destinations and Panaytayan, but a tourism listing for a community is not blanket permission to visit, record or use cultural material. The Mangyan Heritage Center says that the appropriate Mangyan Peoples Organization must give consent for research, direct visits and collaboration. This distinction should be explicit in the app.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: The National Commission for Culture and the Arts records that Ginaw Bilog, a Hanunuo Mangyan poet from Panaytayan, received National Living Treasure recognition in 1993 for helping preserve and share ambahan. Ambahan has seven-syllable lines and is used for expression through metaphors and messages. The Library of Congress also documents historical Mangyan writing on bamboo and its transmission. These are strong sources for education without reproducing entire protected poems, assigning one community’s practices to every group, or assuming performances are public domain. Mansalay’s Mangyan Festival is a public celebration, but not a substitute for community-authored heritage content.

localities.name: Naujan
localities.lead: A historic municipality centered on a major freshwater wetland, fisheries, farming and natural heritage.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Naujan’s municipal-history page reports a Spanish-era town origin, early settlements along the coast and historical interactions with traders and colonial authorities. It also records an explanation of the name associated with nauhaw as local tradition. Specific assertions about the ethnicity of early peoples based on Chinese-origin artifacts are not a sound archaeological inference: trade objects do not prove the identities of all original inhabitants. The historical narrative can instead be taught through settlement patterns, documented administrative changes and careful analysis of what artifacts do and do not establish.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: Naujan Lake National Park has an internationally recognized Ramsar wetland designation. Historical Ramsar information discusses freshwater habitats, migratory and resident birds, fisheries, settlements, rice cultivation, watershed pressures and conservation concerns. The lake landscape is associated with Naujan, Pola, Socorro and Victoria; it should not be presented as belonging solely to Naujan. The official tourism directory also lists water-based and natural attractions and an Alangan Mangyan souvenir-related listing, which is evidence of a listed business, not a population or cultural census.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: The DaBaLisTiHit Festival offers a unique way to interpret wetland life. Organizers explain the name as abbreviations of five fish names—dalag, banak, banglis, tilapia and hito—and use them in props and street dancing. These symbolic references are useful for cultural interpretation but should be separated from current scientific surveys or claims about fish abundance. For community traditions and possible Tadyawan and Alangan connections in the region, local group sources and consent are still needed rather than using a historical wetland map as a contemporary ethnic boundary.

localities.name: Pinamalayan
localities.lead: A town with a rainbow-associated oral origin story and a distinctive planned-town history.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Pinamalayan’s municipal-history account recounts a founding legend of travelers seeing a rainbow as they approached shore. Because it is a narrated origin story, the rainbow should be described as tradition and not verifiable eyewitness history. The same detailed local account describes early settlement at Lumambayan, later movement of the town center and an organized choice between alternative town sites. Road construction, a grid layout, a central plaza and subsequent connectivity are distinctive aspects of Pinamalayan’s recorded twentieth-century development.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The official tourism directory identifies Pinamalayan as a market-and-agriculture-related locality and lists coastal destinations, Cawa-Cawa Falls and routes or parks. The Rainbow-themed Bahaghari Festival carries a public interpretation of the old settlement story through costumes, parades and street dancing. A market and road-building narrative is a stronger way to discuss everyday work and mobility than claiming that every citizen shares an identical oral tradition or festival experience.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Pinamalayan Welcome Arch is listed as a historical-cultural destination. An arch may mark arrival and civic identity, but its design, age and symbolism require site-specific documentation. The local history page reports that choosing the present town center involved public discussion and a vote, an engaging example of community planning as civic heritage. In lesson activities, clearly distinguish the folk rainbow story, the documented changes in settlement design and the actual public Bahaghari Festival calendar.

localities.name: Pola
localities.lead: An east-coast municipality with a river-estuary town center, fishing and nipa-weaving history.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: The provincial local-history account associates Pola’s name with reddish soil and the Tagalog word pula, but this remains a recorded explanation of the place name. It describes the settlement near the Casiligan River estuary and a history of changing administrative ties with Pinamalayan before reestablishment as a separate municipality in the early twentieth century. The reported nineteenth-century and colonial events should be treated as a summarized local history rather than relied upon as a detailed modern chronicle without primary records.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: Pola’s setting includes Pola Bay, the Casiligan River and agricultural and fishing areas. The municipal history specifically mentions nipa weaving among its local livelihood traditions. Its coastal identity and the Sab-Uyan Festival are linked in an annual feast of Saint John the Baptist and a procession associated with the sea. Pola is also connected geographically to the broader Naujan Lake region. This does not make a freshwater conservation site and a coastal religious festival the same thing; they deserve separate source-backed explanations.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: The official cultural directory lists Pola Heritage Houses. They provide a starting point for learning architectural and family history, but the page does not supply each building’s construction date, ownership or style. Learners can compare locally verified architectural evidence with Pola’s reported old town history, fishing livelihoods and nipa materials. Sensitive photographs of lived-in houses or communities should require permission where appropriate. The Sab-Uyan festival description can explain a public Catholic procession but should not be used to imply that every household shares the same faith.

localities.name: Puerto Galera
localities.lead: An historic harbor and trading landscape with a contemporary Iraya cultural festival and waterfront heritage.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Puerto Galera’s detailed municipal-history page describes Minolo and Muelle in accounts of historic trade, strategic anchorage and movement of people or goods around Mindoro. It cites Chinese chronicles and archaeological discoveries, but precise assertions about tenth-century trade routes, artifacts and name derivation need scholarly verification. Muelle’s continued presence as a waterfront place gives learners a tangible question: how can a harbor accumulate layers of travel, trade, military, commercial and local memory across generations? Distinguish historical interpretation from the current tourism role of beaches and diving.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The provincial destination directory lists Muelle Cultural Heritage Park as well as beaches, dive sites and waterfalls. Tourism is a contemporary economic sector, but the harbor’s location and Iraya cultural context make it more than a recreational destination. Learners can compare a port history source, a heritage park listing and a present-day tourism description, then ask how coastal environments influence travel, work and environmental stewardship. Current safety, transport and conservation conditions are not fixed by an offline guide.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Kaaldawan-Iraya Festival is described by public organizers as a celebration recognizing Iraya Mangyan heritage through songs, folktales, dances and games. The Library of Congress and NCCA treat Iraya as distinct from other Mangyan ethnolinguistic communities. The festival page verifies an organizer’s presentation, not the precise meaning, ownership or public-reuse rights of every performance. Any further detailed account of beliefs or living traditional knowledge should be written with authorized Iraya partners and free, prior and informed consent.

localities.name: Roxas
localities.lead: A southern agricultural-trade center whose historical names include Ticling and Paclasan.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Roxas’s long municipal-history page recounts oral accounts of a coastal settler named Isidro, nicknamed Ticling, and a later place called Paclasan. It also describes nineteenth-century farming settlements, movement of families from Panay, Romblon and Batangas, and efforts to separate from Mansalay. The local account associates the formation of the modern municipality with the late 1940s and the name of President Manuel Roxas. Some executive-order numbers and dates in the page appear inconsistent, so they should be verified in official gazettes before quiz publication.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The provincial tourism overview describes Roxas as a hub for southern commerce, agricultural products and services. The SIPAG Festival emphasizes palay and fruits, highlighting the role of farming and trading in public civic identity. The portal lists agricultural tourism destinations as well as Clarendon Cultural Center, which makes it possible to teach the difference between everyday economic activity, a contemporary festival and a named cultural venue. A historical anecdote about how a town was named should remain attributed to a storyteller or source.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Clarendon Cultural Center is listed as a historical and cultural site, but an online directory does not document all exhibitions or give a complete institutional history. The app should allow later insertion of verified objects, cultural practitioners or gallery exhibitions with rights information. Learners could analyze how roads, migration and trading places shaped Roxas’s growth and compare that documented municipal narrative with SIPAG’s public celebration of effort and agricultural work.

localities.name: San Teodoro
localities.lead: A northern municipality previously known as Subaan, shaped by colonial changes and Iraya community connections.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: San Teodoro’s municipal history describes an earlier place called Subaan and a settlement centered near Lumangbayan. It reports changing church and government jurisdiction among Baco, Calapan and Puerto Galera during the Spanish and American periods. Its account of the present name includes more than one historical figure named Theodore, and the text itself expresses uncertainty about a name. It is better to teach how the place-name account reflects changing administrations than to present one unverified definitive etymology.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The public tourism directory lists Punta Baluarte as a heritage site along with falls, rivers, beaches and ecopark destinations. In the northern travel corridor, terrain and coastal routes influence how settlements connect. The MASAYAW Festival highlights faith and lively community participation with street dancing and cultural presentations, but its public summary does not define everyone’s religious practice or social identity. Distinguish a tourist viewpoint, a festival theme and a source documenting residents’ daily lives.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: The Mangyan Heritage Center lists a named Iraya Peoples Organization based in Taisan, San Teodoro, indicating an important present-day Indigenous representation in the town. That listing does not justify mapping every household’s identity or discussing private rituals without permission. Heritage lessons should discuss this as community organizational context and offer opportunities for community-approved content, not imply that an attraction or annual public festival represents all Iraya cultural knowledge.

localities.name: Socorro
localities.lead: A municipality created from part of Pola, adjoining Naujan Lake and marked by harvest-related celebrations.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: Socorro’s provincial history states that the municipality was carved from Pola and that part of its older area was known as Catiningan. It attributes the new municipality to Republic Act No. 3609 in 1963 and documents local political organization and boundary changes later in the decade. This is a distinct modern municipal-history story, and the origin of the name given in the source should remain an attributed account. The history also places Socorro in the central part of the province with Naujan Lake toward the north.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The source describes Socorro as an agricultural municipality, and Naujan Lake adds a separate dimension of freshwater ecology and livelihood in the surrounding region. The historical Ramsar sheet records wetland habitats, fisheries, agriculture and conservation challenges affecting the lake region. The annual Pakapya-Agtike Festival is described by organizers as a harvest thanksgiving occasion. None of these references gives a complete present-day map of where Tadyawan families live or the precise nature of their beliefs.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: The festival’s tourism description says it resembles a Tadyawan Mangyan thanksgiving ritual, which is the organizer’s characterization, not automatically an Indigenous community-authored account. To teach Tadyawan heritage responsibly, obtain statements from the appropriate community People’s Organization and its culture bearers. The app can currently present the documented public performance and learn about wetland conservation without attempting to instruct users in restricted ritual practices or to reproduce songs, prayers or cultural designs.

localities.name: Victoria
localities.lead: A municipality formed from Naujan territory and known for fruit agriculture, with links to the wider lake landscape.

sections.title: History and how the town developed
sections.text: The Victoria municipal-history account describes a local campaign for independent municipality status from Naujan, including community planning for a townsite. It recounts a visit by leaders to President Elpidio Quirino and his daughter Victoria. The site identifies Executive Order No. 620 of September 18, 1953, as organizing the new municipality. The creation narrative helps learners understand how twentieth-century local governance and roads affected civic identity. Specific personal anecdotes in the town chronicle should remain sourced, not portrayed as universal community memory.

sections.title: Landscape and ways of living
sections.text: The official Kapakyanan Festival account emphasizes rice, citrus and other fruits such as rambutan, lanzones and durian. The directory also lists integrated farms, agroecology farms and waterfall-related sites. These sources together can introduce agricultural diversity without claiming exact current output volumes or every resident’s occupation. Victoria is additionally linked with Naujan Lake’s wider wetland region, so its heritage story can compare farms and marketed products with freshwater habitats and water-dependent neighboring communities.

sections.title: Culture, places and what to learn
sections.text: Victoria’s cultural learning should keep the Kapakyanan Festival, modern municipal creation and shared lake stewardship as three distinct topics, not one generic festival paragraph repeated in several sections. Agricultural fairs and trade exhibits are public presentations of produce, while the historical Ramsar report concerns wetlands and conservation. Both can support questions about livelihoods and environmental responsibility. For claims about Mangyan-specific community identities or rituals, the province-wide ethnolinguistic references do not establish precise current town-level boundaries.

festivals.name: Basudani Festival
festivals.description: The festival is presented as thanksgiving for harvest abundance, with street dancing by different sectors of Bansud. The published account connects farming, community participation and municipal identity. It does not establish the occupation or customs of every resident.

festivals.name: SIPAG Festival
festivals.description: SIPAG presents Roxas as a southern trade-and-commerce center and highlights work associated with palay and fruits such as banana, rambutan, lanzones and durian. It celebrates the industriousness described by organizers, rather than claiming that all Roxaseños have identical livelihoods.

festivals.name: Banana Festival
festivals.description: The festival gives thanks for banana harvests and their role in Baco’s agricultural economy. Its provincial background identifies lupakan, harana and pandangguhan as featured cultural activities; the precise form and yearly schedule should be checked with organizers.

festivals.name: SULYOG Festival
festivals.description: SULYOG is explained by organizers as combining suli (a Mangyan-language term linked with banana) and niyog (coconut). Its public celebration includes crop-related presentations, agricultural exhibits and street dancing. Attribution is to the festival’s account, not an authoritative general dictionary of all Mangyan languages.

festivals.name: Kalap Festival
festivals.description: Kalap celebrates Calapan’s civic identity and founding history. The tourism account gives different explanations of kalap, including a tree name and gathering wood, then emphasizes unity and cooperation. Those etymologies are presented as reported interpretations, not as a settled linguistic derivation.

festivals.name: Bahaghari Festival
festivals.description: Pinamalayan’s celebration uses a rainbow theme, linked by local history to a migration-and-settlement narrative. Colorful costumes and a street-dance competition are public features. The rainbow founding narrative should be clearly labeled local oral tradition rather than treated as an archaeological fact.

festivals.name: Pandang Gitab Oriental Mindoro
festivals.description: Pandang Gitab is presented as the province’s Festival of Lights and as a street-dancing thanksgiving celebration. The symbolism of light in the public account expresses hope and solidarity among localities, but it does not imply their cultural traditions are interchangeable.

festivals.name: Sab-Uyan Festival
festivals.description: Associated with the feast of Saint John the Baptist, the festival includes a coastal or fluvial religious procession in Pola. The tourism account connects its setting to the sea, and published descriptions should be attributed to the organizers rather than expanded into undocumented spiritual beliefs.

festivals.name: Pakapya-Agtike Festival
festivals.description: The festival’s official page links Socorro with harvest thanksgiving and an organizer-described presentation inspired by Tadyawan Mangyan traditions, alongside street dancing and cultural performances. The festival description is not a community-approved guide to Tadyawan beliefs or rituals; related explanations require appropriate community review.

festivals.name: Biniray Festival
festivals.description: Biniray is associated in the provincial account with early settlers from Panay, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, and blessings from the sea. It connects religion and maritime livelihoods in a public celebration, including a fluvial procession. Do not treat a general festival narrative as proof of each family’s ancestry.

festivals.name: DABALISTIHIT Festival
festivals.description: The name is explained in the official account through freshwater fish: dalag (Da), banak (Ba), banglis (Lis), tilapia (Ti) and hito (Hit). Fish-themed costumes and props connect the public performance to Naujan Lake. The celebration is not a current biodiversity census.

festivals.name: Kapakyanan Festival
festivals.description: The festival’s public account highlights rice production and citrus or tropical fruits, naming rambutan, lanzones and durian among the area’s products. Agricultural fairs and public performances connect crops and trade to Victoria’s identity; verify any current-market figures separately.

festivals.name: Kawayanan Festival
festivals.description: Kawayanan emphasizes bamboo and the uses of this material in daily life. The provincial festival page connects it with a town that also produces rice and coconut; craft displays and performances showcase public material culture. A bamboo craft should not automatically be identified as a specific Indigenous ceremonial item.

festivals.name: Kaaldawan-Iraya Festival
festivals.description: The public festival is described as recognizing Iraya Mangyan heritage through showcased songs, games, folktales, dances and cultural presentations. It should not be mistaken for permission to record or republish community stories; Iraya traditions must be explained with community attribution and consent.

festivals.name: Fiesta MAHAL TANA!
festivals.description: A provincial festival showcase in Calapan involving contingents from Oriental Mindoro’s 14 municipalities and one component city. It presents many celebrations within one event, while each municipality’s historical and cultural specificity remains distinct.

festivals.name: Salong Dagitab Festival
festivals.description: A provincial night celebration that emphasizes light displays and Christmas decorations, with participation by government offices, institutions and communities. It differs from Pandang Gitab, which the official portal defines as a separate provincial Festival of Lights.

festivals.description: The Mansalay festival is publicly described as recognizing local Mangyan cultural heritage through presentations, dances and crafts. However, the label covers distinct communities and any representations of knowledge, ritual or designs must be checked with the relevant community Peoples Organizations.
